---
title: "Area-Level Estimation"
subtitle: "Bayesian Fay-Herriot models with area predictors, year effects, and spatial structure"
---

Area-level SAE starts from the direct estimates created in the previous workbook. The Fay--Herriot model lets direct estimates for each MSOA--year borrow strength from predictors and spatial and temporal structures to stabilise noisy estimates of **share of adults who walk for transport daily, by MSOA-year**. The goal is to see what changes as we add more auxiliary information to the model

```{r}
#| label: setup-area-level
library(dplyr)
library(readr)
library(stringr)
library(tidyr)
library(sf)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)
library(spdep)
library(INLA)

base_path <- here::here("data")

share_label <- scales::label_percent(accuracy = 1)
pp_label <- scales::label_number(accuracy = 1, scale = 100, suffix = " pp")
variance_label <- scales::label_number(accuracy = 0.001)

msoa_boundaries <- st_read(
  file.path(base_path, "boundaries-msoa.geojson"),
  quiet = TRUE
) |>
  rename(domain_id = all_of("MSOA21CD")) |>
  filter(str_starts(.data$domain_id, "W")) |>
  arrange(.data$domain_id)
```
## Prepare data for modelling

First we imported the direct estimates computed in the previous step, together with their sampling variances for all MSOA--year combinations.  We will also load the prepared dataset of normalised area predictors for daily walking, from which the models will borrow strengths from to stabilise the estimates.

```{r}
#| label: load-area-inputs
direct_walk <- read_csv(
  file.path(base_path, "freq_walker_estimates_direct.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

area_covariates <- read_csv(
  file.path(base_path, "clean", "area_covariates_daily_walking.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
) |>
  rename(domain_id = all_of("msoa_code")) |>
  select(
    all_of(c(
      "domain_id",
      "cov_population_density",
      "cov_share_no_car_households",
      "cov_share_work_from_home",
      "cov_share_students",
      "cov_share_routine_semiroutine"
    ))
  )

model_data_raw <- direct_walk |>
  left_join(area_covariates, by = "domain_id")

head(model_data_raw)
```

Before fitting the models, we create a consistent numeric index for each MSOA and survey year. These indices are used by INLA to attach random effects to the correct area and period. 

```{r}
#| label: define-model-index
#| code-fold: false

area_levels <- sort(unique(model_data_raw[["domain_id"]]))
year_levels <- sort(unique(model_data_raw[["wave_year"]]))

area_index <- tibble::tibble(
  domain_id = area_levels,
  area_id = seq_along(area_levels)
)

year_index <- tibble::tibble(
  wave_year = year_levels,
  year_id = seq_along(year_levels)
)
```

Model M4 includes a spatial random effect, so we also need an adjacency graph `.adj` as INLA input. We use Queen contiguity, where two MSOAs are treated as neighbours if their boundaries touch at either an edge or a point. The boundary file is sorted using `area_index` so that the graph order matches the area IDs used in the modelling data.

![](../assets/spatial_weights_example.png)

```{r}
#| label: build-spatial-graph
#| code-fold: false

msoa_boundaries_sorted <- msoa_boundaries |>
  dplyr::inner_join(area_index, by = "domain_id") |>
  dplyr::arrange(.data$area_id)

msoa_neighbours <- spdep::poly2nb(
  msoa_boundaries_sorted,
  queen = TRUE,
  row.names = msoa_boundaries_sorted$domain_id
)

spatial_graph_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".adj")

spdep::nb2INLA(
  file = spatial_graph_file,
  nb = msoa_neighbours
)
```

We then assemble the modelling data. The models use two area-level random-effect structures, so we create separate INLA index variables:

- `area_iid_id` indexes the unstructured, independent area effect.
- `area_spatial_id` indexes the structured spatial area effect, which uses the   adjacency graph.

The sampling variance also needs careful handling before fitting the FH models. Because the outcome is binary (`1` for walking daily, `0` otherwise), small MSOA-year samples can produce direct estimates with very low, zero, or missing variance. If untreated, those would be treated as overly precise. To avoid this, we apply a minimum sampling-variance floor. For MSOA-year unit without a direct estimate, we assign a large variance value of `1`, signalling high uncertainty.

```{r}
#| label: prepare-model-data
#| code-fold: false

sampling_variance_floor <- quantile(
  model_data_raw$variance[model_data_raw$variance > 0],
  probs = 0.05,
  na.rm = TRUE,
  names = FALSE
)

model_data <- model_data_raw |>
  left_join(area_index, by = "domain_id") |>
  left_join(year_index, by = "wave_year") |>
  mutate(
    area_iid_id = area_id,
    area_spatial_id = area_id,
    sampling_variance = case_when(
      # No direct estimate: treat as maximum uncertainty.
      is.na(direct_estimate) ~ 1,
      # Missing or tiny variances get the same lower bound.
      is.na(variance) ~ sampling_variance_floor,
      TRUE ~ pmax(variance, sampling_variance_floor)
    )
  ) |>
  arrange(wave_year, area_id)

head(model_data)
```

## Fit Models

Each model uses the direct estimate as the response. The sampling variance from the direct-estimation workbook is passed to INLA as known observation-level uncertainty, so cells with noisy direct estimates receive less weight.

We will fit five cumulative models:

| Model | Name | Specifications |
|---|---|---|
| M0 | Baseline | Intercept plus independent MSOA random effect |
| M1 | +Temporal | M0 plus year (random walk) |
| M2 | +Core predictors | M1 plus population density and no-car households |
| M3 | +All predictors | M2 plus economic activities (full-time students, semi-routine/routine occupation, WFH) |
| M4 | +Spatial | M3 plus spatial structure (among MSOA adjacency) |

First, we define the model specifications and fit each one to the direct estimates. 

```{r}
#| label: fit-fh-models
#| code-fold: false

m0_formula <- direct_estimate ~
  1 +
  f(area_iid_id, model = "iid")

m1_formula <- direct_estimate ~
  1 +
  f(area_iid_id, model = "iid") +
  f(year_id, model = "rw1", constr = TRUE)

m2_formula <- direct_estimate ~
  cov_population_density +
  cov_share_no_car_households +
  f(area_iid_id, model = "iid") +
  f(year_id, model = "rw1", constr = TRUE)

m3_formula <- direct_estimate ~
  cov_population_density +
  cov_share_no_car_households +
  cov_share_work_from_home +
  cov_share_students +
  cov_share_routine_semiroutine +
  f(area_iid_id, model = "iid") +
  f(year_id, model = "rw1", constr = TRUE)

m4_formula <- direct_estimate ~
  cov_population_density +
  cov_share_no_car_households +
  cov_share_work_from_home +
  cov_share_students +
  cov_share_routine_semiroutine +
  f(
    area_spatial_id,
    model = "bym2",
    graph = spatial_graph_file,
    scale.model = TRUE,
    constr = TRUE
  ) +
  f(year_id, model = "rw1", constr = TRUE)

model_formulas <- list(
  "M0 Baseline" = m0_formula,
  "M1 +Temporal" = m1_formula,
  "M2 +Core predictors" = m2_formula,
  "M3 +All predictors" = m3_formula,
  "M4 +Spatial" = m4_formula
)
```
Then, we fit the FH models using INLA

```{r}
#| label: fit-fh-func
#| code-fold: false
#|
fit_fh_model <- function(formula) {
  INLA::inla(
    formula = formula,
    family = "gaussian",
    data = model_data,
    scale = 1 / model_data$sampling_variance,
    control.family = list(
      hyper = list(
        prec = list(initial = 0, fixed = TRUE)
      )
    ),
    control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE),
    control.compute = list(dic = TRUE, waic = TRUE),
    verbose = FALSE
  )
}

model_order <- names(model_formulas)
fh_fits <- lapply(model_formulas, fit_fh_model)
```

At this point the result is just a named list of fitted INLA models. We will collate the fitted values into one results table together with their direct estimates and variances. 

```{r}
#| label: collate-fh-results

# Main frame to keep from model data
output_cols <- c(
  "domain_id",
  "wave_year",
  "msoa_name",
  "direct_estimate",
  "variance",
  "n"
)

model_output_frame <- select(model_data, all_of(output_cols))

# Extract fitted values from each model and bind them to the frame
fh_result_tables <- purrr::map2(
  fh_fits,
  names(fh_fits),
  function(fit, model_name) {
    fitted_values <- tibble::as_tibble(fit$summary.fitted.values)

    model_results <- bind_cols(model_output_frame, fitted_values)

    transmute(
      model_results,
      model = model_name,
      across(all_of(output_cols)),
      fh_estimate = .data$mean,
      fh_variance = .data$sd^2,
      has_direct = !is.na(.data$direct_estimate)
    )
  }
)

# Stack model outputs and set display order
fh_results <- bind_rows(fh_result_tables)
fh_results <- mutate(
  fh_results,
  model = factor(.data$model, levels = model_order)
)

head(fh_results)
```

## Compare Models

We start by looking at what changes when we move from the direct estimates to Model 0. M0 is the baseline Fay-Herriot model: no covariates, no temporal effect, and no spatial structure. It is useful because it shows what partial pooling alone does to the noisy direct estimates.

MSOA-years with high direct-estimate variance contain less local information, so the model pulls them more strongly towards the overall pattern. Cells with missing or zero direct-estimate variance can also regain uncertainty in the model output, because they should not be treated as genuinely precise just because the direct variance is unavailable or degenerate.

```{r}
share_label <- scales::label_percent(accuracy = 0.1)
pp_label <- scales::label_number(accuracy = 0.1, scale = 100, suffix = " pp")
variance_label <- scales::label_number(accuracy = 0.01)

map_text_theme <- theme(
  plot.title = element_text(size = 18, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
  strip.text = element_text(size = 15, face = "bold"),
  legend.title = element_text(size = 13),
  legend.text = element_text(size = 12)
)

chart_text_theme <- theme(
  plot.title = element_text(size = 18, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
  strip.text = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold"),
  axis.title = element_text(size = 14),
  axis.text = element_text(size = 12),
  legend.text = element_text(size = 12)
)
```
```{r}
#| label: direct-to-m0-comparison
#| fig-width: 16
#| fig-height: 10
#| out-width: "100%"

fh_wide <- fh_results |>
  # One row per MSOA-year, with model outputs in separate columns.
  select(
    domain_id,
    wave_year,
    model,
    direct_estimate,
    variance,
    fh_estimate,
    fh_variance
  ) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = model,
    values_from = c(fh_estimate, fh_variance),
    names_sep = "__"
  )

direct_to_m0 <- fh_wide |>
  transmute(
    domain_id,
    wave_year,
    direct_variance = variance,
    variance_change = direct_variance - .data[["fh_variance__M0 Baseline"]]
  )

variance_change_limit <- max(abs(direct_to_m0$variance_change), na.rm = TRUE) * .5
direct_variance_limit <- max(direct_to_m0$direct_variance, na.rm = TRUE)

direct_to_m0_map_data <- msoa_boundaries |>
  left_join(direct_to_m0, by = "domain_id")

shrinkage_maps <- ggplot(direct_to_m0_map_data) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = .data$variance_change), colour = "transparent") +
  facet_wrap(vars(.data$wave_year), nrow = 1) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = "#2166ac",
    mid = "white",
    high = "#762a83",
    midpoint = 0,
    limits = c(-variance_change_limit, variance_change_limit),
    labels = variance_label,
    na.value = "grey85",
    name = "Change"
  ) +
  labs(title = "Variance change from direct estimate to M0") +
  theme_void() +
  map_text_theme

direct_variance_maps <- ggplot(direct_to_m0_map_data) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = .data$direct_variance), colour = "transparent") +
  facet_wrap(vars(.data$wave_year), nrow = 1) +
  scale_fill_distiller(
    palette = "Reds",
    direction = 1,
    limits = c(0, direct_variance_limit),
    labels = variance_label,
    na.value = "grey85",
    name = "Variance"
  ) +
  labs(title = "Direct-estimate variance") +
  theme_void() +
  map_text_theme


direct_to_m0_ranked <- direct_to_m0 |>
  filter(!is.na(variance_change)) |>
  group_by(wave_year) |>
  # Rank within each wave by the original direct-estimate variance.
  arrange(direct_variance, .by_group = TRUE) |>
  mutate(variance_rank = row_number()) |>
  ungroup() |>
  select(
    wave_year,
    variance_rank,
    `Variance change` = variance_change,
    `Variance (direct)` = direct_variance
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -c(wave_year, variance_rank),
    names_to = "measure",
    values_to = "value"
  )

direct_to_m0_ranked_plot <- ggplot(
  direct_to_m0_ranked,
  aes(
    x = .data$variance_rank,
    y = .data$value,
    colour = .data$measure
  )
) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(vars(.data$wave_year), nrow = 1) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = variance_label) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(
    "Variance change" = "purple",
    "Variance (direct)" = "red"
  )) +
  labs(
    title = "",
    x = "MSOAs sorted by variance",
    y = "Variance",
    colour = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  chart_text_theme

shrinkage_maps / direct_variance_maps / direct_to_m0_ranked_plot +
  plot_layout(heights = c(1, 1, 1))
```

Next we compare the fitted models using WAIC, returned by `INLA()`. WAIC tells us how well each model is expected to predict new data, while also penalising models that are more complex. 

Based on WAIC (lower is better), M0 is weaker than the models that add more area-level information. M2 has the lowest WAIC in this run, suggesting that the two core predictors, population density and car access, capture much of the global area-level variability, although the differences among M1-M4 are small.

```{r}
#| label: waic-comparison
model_waic <- purrr::imap_dfr(
  fh_fits,
  \(fit, model_name) {
    tibble::tibble(
      model = model_name,
      waic = fit$waic$waic,
      eff_params = fit$waic$p.eff
    )
  }
) 

model_waic
```

WAIC is a global check, so it does not show where the model changes locally. To understand what the additional predictors and spatio-temporal terms are doing, we also look at how the MSOA-level estimates are adjusted at each step.

When moving from M2 to M3, we add the extra occupation and work-pattern predictors. The first row maps how much the estimates change after adding those predictors. The second row shows the direction of shrinkage using the change in absolute residuals. Negative values, seen in parts of southern and central Wales, suggest that the additional predictors in M3 help recover local variation that was previously smoothed away in M2.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 16
#| fig-height: 9
#| out-width: "100%"

m2_to_m3 <- fh_wide |>
  transmute(
    domain_id,
    wave_year,
    estimate_change =
      .data[["fh_estimate__M3 +All predictors"]] -
      .data[["fh_estimate__M2 +Core predictors"]],
    abs_residual_change =
      abs(.data$direct_estimate - .data[["fh_estimate__M3 +All predictors"]]) -
      abs(.data$direct_estimate - .data[["fh_estimate__M2 +Core predictors"]])
  )

m2_to_m3_map_data <- msoa_boundaries |>
  left_join(m2_to_m3, by = "domain_id")

m2_to_m3_estimate_limit <- quantile(
  abs(m2_to_m3$estimate_change),
  0.95,
  na.rm = TRUE,
  names = FALSE
)

m2_to_m3_residual_limit <- quantile(
  abs(m2_to_m3$abs_residual_change),
  0.95,
  na.rm = TRUE,
  names = FALSE
)

m2_to_m3_estimate_map <- ggplot(m2_to_m3_map_data) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = .data$estimate_change), colour = "transparent") +
  facet_wrap(vars(.data$wave_year), nrow = 1) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = "#2166ac",
    mid = "white",
    high = "#b2182b",
    midpoint = 0,
    limits = c(-m2_to_m3_estimate_limit, m2_to_m3_estimate_limit),
    oob = scales::squish,
    labels = pp_label,
    na.value = "grey85",
    name = "Change"
  ) +
  labs(title = "Estimate change after adding additional predictors") +
  theme_void() +
  map_text_theme

m2_to_m3_shrinkage_map <- ggplot(m2_to_m3_map_data) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = .data$abs_residual_change), colour = "transparent") +
  facet_wrap(vars(.data$wave_year), nrow = 1) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = "purple",
    mid = "white",
    high = "orange",
    midpoint = 0,
    limits = c(-m2_to_m3_residual_limit, m2_to_m3_residual_limit),
    oob = scales::squish,
    labels = pp_label,
    na.value = "grey85",
    name = "Change"
  ) +
  labs(title = "Shift relative to direct estimates after adding predictors") +
  theme_void() +
  map_text_theme

m2_to_m3_estimate_map / m2_to_m3_shrinkage_map +
  plot_layout(heights = c(1, 1))
```

Finally, we look at the spatio-temporal terms through two hyperparameters returned by `INLA()`: `tau` and `phi`.

- `tau` is the precision of the random effect; higher means less variation. The temporal random effect helps the model account for differences between survey waves, and its high `tau` suggests that those differences exist but are not very large. On the other hand, spatial `tau` is lower, suggesting more residual variation between MSOAs than between years.

```{r}
#| label: m4-tau
fh_fits[["M4 +Spatial"]]$summary.hyperpar |>
  tibble::as_tibble(rownames = "parameter") |>
  dplyr::filter(stringr::str_detect(.data$parameter, "Precision")) |>
  dplyr::select(parameter, mean, sd, `0.025quant`, `0.5quant`, `0.975quant`)
```

- `phi` is the share of the BYM2 random-effect variance account for by the structured spatial component. The low `phi` shows that only a small share of that variation is spatially structured.

```{r}
#| label: m4-spatial-phi
fh_fits[["M4 +Spatial"]]$summary.hyperpar |>
  tibble::as_tibble(rownames = "parameter") |>
  dplyr::filter(stringr::str_detect(.data$parameter, "Phi")) |>
  dplyr::select(parameter, mean, sd, `0.025quant`, `0.5quant`, `0.975quant`)
```
In reality, this means the spatial structure is more likely to matter in specific places than across the whole model. We compare M3 and M4 to see where spatial smoothing changes the estimates. Spatial smoothing lowers estimates in parts of the north and raises estimates in the more urban south, suggesting that the spatial term is making very local adjustments.

```{r}
#| label: spatial-change-map
#| fig-width: 16
#| fig-height: 9
#| out-width: "100%"

m3_to_m4 <- fh_wide |>
  transmute(
    domain_id,
    wave_year,
    estimate_change =
      .data[["fh_estimate__M4 +Spatial"]] -
      .data[["fh_estimate__M3 +All predictors"]],
    abs_residual_change =
      abs(.data$direct_estimate - .data[["fh_estimate__M4 +Spatial"]]) -
      abs(.data$direct_estimate - .data[["fh_estimate__M3 +All predictors"]])
  )

m3_to_m4_map_data <- msoa_boundaries |>
  left_join(m3_to_m4, by = "domain_id")

m3_to_m4_limit <- quantile(
  abs(m3_to_m4$estimate_change),
  0.95,
  na.rm = TRUE,
  names = FALSE
)

m3_to_m4_estimate_map <- ggplot(m3_to_m4_map_data) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = .data$estimate_change), colour = "transparent") +
  facet_wrap(vars(.data$wave_year), nrow = 1) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = "#2166ac",
    mid = "white",
    high = "#b2182b",
    midpoint = 0,
    limits = c(-m3_to_m4_limit, m3_to_m4_limit),
    oob = scales::squish,
    labels = pp_label,
    na.value = "grey85",
    name = "Change"
  ) +
  labs(title = "Estimate change after adding spatial smoothing") +
  theme_void() +
  map_text_theme

```

## Final Model

We use M4 as the final model. Although M2 has the lowest WAIC, i.e., high predictive power, the differences among M1-M4 are small. M4 stays close to the best WAIC model while allowing local estimates to borrow information from additional predictors and neighbouring MSOAs for extra smoothing.

Final estimates show higher estimated daily-walking shares in several urban areas of south Wales, with lower estimates across many rural and suburban areas. Even after the direct estimates have been stabilised through the FH model, some MSOA-years still have high posterior variance. The final estimates should therefore be reported alongside their uncertainty so that downstream operations can distinguish areas with similar estimated daily-walking rates but very different levels of certainty.


```{r}
#| label: final-model-map
#| fig-width: 16
#| fig-height: 8
#| out-width: "100%"

# Keep only the final, most structured model.
final_model_results <- fh_results |>
  filter(.data$model == "M4 +Spatial")

final_map_data <- msoa_boundaries |>
  left_join(final_model_results, by = "domain_id")

final_estimate_limits <- range(final_model_results$fh_estimate, na.rm = TRUE)
final_variance_limits <- c(0, max(final_model_results$fh_variance, na.rm = TRUE))

# Map posterior means and variance
estimate_maps <- ggplot(final_map_data) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = .data$fh_estimate), colour = "transparent") +
  facet_wrap(vars(.data$wave_year)) +
  scale_fill_distiller(
    palette = "Blues",
    direction = 1,
    limits = final_estimate_limits,
    labels = share_label,
    na.value = "grey85",
    name = "Share"
  ) +
  labs(title = "Final FH estimate") +
  theme_void() +
  map_text_theme

uncertainty_maps <- ggplot(final_map_data) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = .data$fh_variance), colour = "transparent") +
  facet_wrap(vars(.data$wave_year)) +
  scale_fill_distiller(
    palette = "Oranges",
    direction = 1,
    limits = final_variance_limits,
    labels = variance_label,
    na.value = "grey85",
    name = "Variance"
  ) +
  labs(title = "Posterior variance") +
  theme_void() +
  map_text_theme

estimate_maps / uncertainty_maps  +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "Frequent walking: M4 spatio-temporal model with 5 predictors",
    theme = theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 20, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5))
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: export-fh-results
#| echo: false
write_csv(
  fh_results,
  file.path(base_path, "freq_walker_estimates_fh_inla.csv")
)

local_change_diagnostics <- bind_rows(
  m2_to_m3 |>
    mutate(comparison = "M2 to M3", .before = 1),
  m3_to_m4 |>
    mutate(comparison = "M3 to M4", .before = 1)
)

write_csv(
  local_change_diagnostics,
  file.path(base_path, "freq_walker_fh_step_diagnostics.csv")
)
```
